books.section: The Rise of the Service Sector
Prosperity and a New World Order (1988–2000)

stem: Which of the following most likely contributed to the trend shown in the chart?

options.text: The spread of air conditioning across the Sun Belt
options.misconception: Air conditioning moved people and plants south, but that shifts jobs within the country, not out of factory work.

options.text: The building of the Interstate Highway System in the 1950s
options.misconception: The highways were built in the 1950s, before this chart's slide, and they helped factories more than they hurt them.

options.text: Rising farm productivity after World War II
options.misconception: Farm productivity shrank farm jobs in an earlier era; it does not explain factory jobs after 1970.

options.text: Automation and firms moving production to lower-wage countries

rationales.A: Sun Belt growth moved jobs within the United States. Background: the national factory share fell anyway, so the cause lay elsewhere.
rationales.B: The highway system dates to the 1950s, two decades before the slide. Background: it spread factories out; it did not shrink them.
rationales.C: Farm productivity explains the earlier fall in farm jobs. Background: this chart tracks factory jobs after 1970.
rationales.D: Background: machines replaced workers on the line, and firms moved production abroad to lower-wage countries; the books name both forces.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what can shrink factory jobs across the whole country at once: something that changes how goods are made, or where.
2. Background: automation let factories produce more with fewer hands, and offshoring moved the work abroad.
3. Test the local answers: air conditioning and highways moved jobs around the map, not out of the sector.
4. The forty-year slide fits forces that never let up, not one dated event.
Remember: when the work itself moves or machines take it, the jobs share falls everywhere at once.
